lessonInput.title: Personas
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence. Claim 2: User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests. Claim 3: Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs. Claim 4: Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

anchors.quote: user profiles or personas that describe groups of users with similar behaviour and needs
Present what you've learned in a way that's easy for others to understand and share.
User needs tend to be high-level, broad in scope and stable over time.
These describe the specific features and content you need to create for your service to meet your users' needs.
This traceability allows you to track related activities and determine how well you're meeting a particular user need.

keyTerms.mi: A research-based persona describes individual interface requests.

keyTerms.df: User needs are higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.

scenario.su: A team must classify passages as user needs or individual interface requests while keeping design choices connected to evidence. A deadline constrains review, and the classification must follow wording about level and stability over time.
scenario.ma: passage describing a higher-level need stable over time, passage stating an individual interface request, notation linking a user story to its source need

mc.q: A team compares a shareable profile of a user group with a statement that is higher-level and more stable over time. Which distinction between a research-based persona and user needs fits those observations?
op: Persona is higher-level; needs profile a user group
Persona describes features; needs present research findings
Persona profiles a user group; needs are higher-level
Persona presents research findings; needs profile user groups
mc.ex: A research-based persona profiles a user group, while user needs are higher-level and more stable than interface requests. Higher-level describes user needs, not the persona.

mc.q: Under a deadline, a team reviews a user story, its source need, and a notation connecting them before evaluating whether the need is met. Which action matches the records?
op: Keep the story linked to its source need
Use the need to describe features and content
Use the story to present research findings
Keep the need linked to its source story
mc.ex: Keeping the user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is met. The specified direction connects the story to its source need, not the need to a source story.

facts: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

keyTerms.df: A shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
keyTerms.eg: A profile detailing the needs of a group of users who exhibit similar behavior.
keyTerms.mi: A research-based persona is just a list of individual user interface requests.
keyTerms.cx: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.

keyTerms.df: Higher-level and more stable requirements that exist over time, distinct from individual interface requests.
keyTerms.eg: A need for a system to be accessible to all users.
keyTerms.mi: User needs are the same as individual interface requests made by a single user.
keyTerms.cx: User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.

keyTerms.df: Descriptions of features and content intended to meet user needs, which are derived from user needs.
keyTerms.eg: A user story describing a feature that allows users to complete a task.
keyTerms.mi: User stories are the same as the high-level user needs themselves.
keyTerms.cx: Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.

scenario.su: A design team is developing a new application and needs to prioritize features based on user research findings. The team has identified a core user need for improved navigation, but they are struggling to connect specific interface requirements to the broader research findings. The constraint is that the team must ensure every feature developed can be traced back to a validated user need.
scenario.ma: Compare the user needs and user stories for the navigation feature, the accessibility feature, and the content update feature.

mc.q: When a team translates user needs into user stories, what is the primary function of this process in relation to the original needs?
op: User stories define individual interface requests
User stories are a way to present research findings
User stories describe features intended to meet needs
User stories are stable over time
mc.ex: Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs. User stories describe features intended to meet needs, which is the correct application of the process.

mc.q: A stakeholder asks how to evaluate if a specific design choice is valid based on the research conducted, and what element connects the design to the research?
op: The design choice must match individual interface requests
The design choice must be stable over time
The design choice must be linked to the source need
The design choice must be a high-level need
mc.ex: Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met, which is the mechanism connecting design to research.

lessonInput.title: Interval number and quality
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.

Claim 1: Four semitones form a major third, while three semitones form a minor third when each spans three scale steps. claims: A written interval is identified by its diatonic span and semitone distance, which together determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished.
Four semitones form a major third, while three semitones form a minor third when each spans three scale steps.

anchors.quote: Intervals were assigned labels based on the scale from which they arose.
four diatonic half-steps is referred to as a major third, while that of three half-steps is a minor third

anchors.loc: 25 Common Practice Era Scales, Other Interval Names
anchors.quote: their specific spellings can indicate different contexts and possible resolutions

facts: A written interval is identified by its diatonic span and semitone distance, which together determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

A tritone can be spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, and the spelling can imply different resolutions.

keyTerms.df: A written interval belongs to a category identified through its diatonic span and semitone distance.
keyTerms.eg: A written interval spanning three scale steps and four semitones is a major third.
keyTerms.mi: The label of a written interval determines its diatonic span and semitone distance.
keyTerms.cx: Its recorded span and semitone count establish whether the label is major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

keyTerms.df: A major third is an interval formed by four semitones across three scale steps.
keyTerms.eg: Four semitones spanning three scale steps provide a concrete major third.
keyTerms.mi: Three semitones across three scale steps identify a major third.
keyTerms.cx: With that three-step span, a three-semitone distance produces a minor third.

keyTerms.df: A tritone is an interval that can carry the spelling augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
keyTerms.eg: A tritone appears once as an augmented fourth and once as a diminished fifth.
keyTerms.mi: A tritone must receive a major or minor label.
keyTerms.cx: Augmented fourth and diminished fifth are the supplied spellings for this interval.

scenario.su: A student must label two written intervals before a deadline using the recorded spans, semitone counts, and spellings. One notation spans three scale steps and measures four semitones; the other is a tritone spelled as a diminished fifth, and the student must distinguish their labels.
scenario.ma: the three-scale-step notation with its four-semitone measurement, the tritone passage bearing the diminished-fifth spelling

mc.q: Two written intervals display different diatonic spans and semitone distances, yet a student proposes assigning labels from the spans alone. Which distinction matches the recorded evidence?
op: Diatonic span and semitone distance determine labels
Labels determine diatonic span and semitone distance
Diatonic span determines labels and semitone distance
Semitone distance determines labels and diatonic span
mc.ex: A written interval's diatonic span and semitone distance together determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished. Reversing that relationship incorrectly treats the label as determining the recorded properties.

mc.q: A written interval spans three scale steps and measures four semitones; with the label due immediately, which classification is supported by the recorded span and distance?
op: Four semitones form a major third
Three semitones form a major third
Four semitones form a minor third
Three scale steps form a minor third
mc.ex: Four semitones across three scale steps form a major third. A minor third instead uses three semitones across that three-step span.

facts: A written interval is identified by its diatonic span and semitone distance, which together determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

keyTerms.cx: The diatonic span is determined by the diatonic span and semitone distance together which determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

keyTerms.mi: The semitone distance is the number of scale steps used to define the interval's quality.
keyTerms.cx: The semitone distance is the semitone distance and diatonic span together which determine labels such as major, minor, augmented, or diminished.

keyTerms.df: The tritone spelling is a way a tritone can be spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, and the spelling can imply different resolutions.
keyTerms.eg: A tritone can be spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, and the spelling can imply different resolutions.
keyTerms.mi: The tritone spelling only refers to the semitone distance used to spell the interval.
keyTerms.cx: The tritone spelling refers to a tritone can be spelled as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, and the spelling can imply different resolutions.

scenario.su: A composer is analyzing a written interval in a piece of music and needs to determine its quality based on its structure. The composer observes an interval spanning four semitones and notes that it is written using three scale steps. The constraint is that the analysis must rely only on the provided claims to distinguish between major and minor thirds.
scenario.ma: The composer compares the interval spanning four semitones to the interval spanning three scale steps to determine the correct label.

mc.q: When analyzing an interval spanning three scale steps, what is the resulting quality based on the provided claims?
op: Three scale steps form a major third
Three scale steps form a minor third

op: Diminished fifth implies a major third
Diminished fifth implies an augmented fourth

lessonInput.title: Electric field
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space. Claim 1: The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate. Claim 2: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

claims: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

anchors.quote: The electric field is the electric force per unit charge.
the direction of the force on a positive test charge
closer field lines indicate a stronger field

facts: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is a description of electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
keyTerms.eg: A positive test charge would accelerate in the direction of the electric field.
keyTerms.mi: Electric field direction is indicated by field-line density.
keyTerms.cx: A positive test charge's acceleration supplies the stated direction, while field-line density concerns relative strength.

keyTerms.df: A positive test charge is the charge referenced per unit when electric force describes an electric field.
keyTerms.eg: Its acceleration direction can be compared with the direction of the electric field.
keyTerms.mi: A positive test charge would accelerate in the direction indicated by field-line density.
keyTerms.cx: Its acceleration follows the electric field direction; density indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: Field-line density is a field-line property distinguished by its indication of relative field strength.
keyTerms.eg: One notation names Field-line density, while another names electric field direction.
keyTerms.mi: Field-line density indicates the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
keyTerms.cx: Density indicates relative strength; positive test charge acceleration provides the field-direction relation.

scenario.su: A workshop group must classify three notations as describing electric field, electric field direction, or relative field strength. Two proposed labels swap direction and relative strength, and the group must resolve the disagreement before the workshop ends.
scenario.ma: electric force per unit positive test charge notation, positive test charge acceleration-direction observation, Field-line density comparison

mc.q: At a point in space, a notation reports electric force per unit positive test charge, while an arrow reports positive test charge acceleration. Which comparison correctly distinguishes electric field description from direction?
op: Field: electric force per unit positive test charge; direction: acceleration.
Field: acceleration direction; direction: force per positive test charge.
Field: field-line density; direction: relative field strength.
Field: relative field strength; direction: field-line density.
mc.ex: Electric force per unit positive test charge describes the electric field, while positive test charge acceleration gives its direction. Field-line density instead indicates relative field strength, not field direction.

mc.q: A field-line sketch shows greater density in region A than region B, and the group must choose a supported label despite competing annotations. Which label follows from the density comparison?
op: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.
Acceleration direction indicates relative field strength.
Field-line density indicates positive test charge direction.
Electric force per unit charge indicates field-line density.
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength. Positive test charge acceleration indicates electric field direction; it does not indicate relative field strength.

facts: An electric field describes the electric force per unit positive test charge at each point in space.
The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate.
Field-line density indicates relative field strength.

keyTerms.df: An electric field is defined as the electric force per unit positive test charge existing at every point in space.
keyTerms.eg: The electric field at a specific location dictates the force a positive test charge would experience there.
keyTerms.mi: The electric field is the total electric force acting on a charge at a given point.
keyTerms.cx: The electric field is specifically the force per unit positive test charge, not the total force acting on a charge.

keyTerms.df: The electric force per unit positive test charge is what an electric field fundamentally describes at any location.
keyTerms.eg: If a positive test charge is placed in a region, the electric force it experiences is described by the electric field.
keyTerms.mi: The electric force is the total interaction between two charges in space.
keyTerms.cx: The electric force per unit positive test charge is the specific quantity that defines the electric field.

keyTerms.df: The density of field lines serves as a measure of the relative field strength at a particular point.
keyTerms.eg: A region with closely packed field lines shows a higher field-line density, indicating a stronger field.
keyTerms.mi: Field-line density is a measure of the total electric field magnitude at a location.
keyTerms.cx: Field-line density specifically indicates the relative field strength, not the total electric field magnitude.

scenario.su: A positive test charge is placed near a region where the electric field is known to be non-zero. The goal is to determine the direction of the resulting acceleration for this charge. The constraint is that the analysis must rely solely on the properties of the electric field.
scenario.ma: The positive test charge is placed at point A, and the electric field vector at point A is measured as pointing toward the positive x-axis. The second inspectable detail is the observation that the field-line density at point B is significantly higher than at point C.

mc.q: When comparing the electric field at two points, how does the field-line density relate to the electric force per unit positive test charge?
op: Field-line density indicates relative field strength.
Field-line density is the direction of acceleration.
Field-line density describes the total electric force.
Field-line density is the electric force per unit charge.
mc.ex: Field-line density indicates relative field strength, then correct the closest distractor which describes the electric force per unit charge.

mc.q: A positive test charge is observed accelerating in a specific direction; what property of the electric field describes this observed acceleration?
op: The electric field is the direction of acceleration.
The electric field is the force per unit charge.
The electric field is the total electric force.
The electric field is the field-line density.
mc.ex: The direction of the electric field is the direction a positive test charge would accelerate, then correct the closest distractor which describes the field-line density.

lessonInput.title: Minor-scale variants
lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: The minor key system has natural, harmonic, and melodic variants that differ through alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees. Claim 1: Harmonic minor raises the seventh scale degree so it can function as a leading tone. Claim 2: Melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
lessonInput.readings: Justin Rubin, Music Composition & Theory (2024), chapter 25, University of Minnesota Libraries Publishing

claims: The minor key system has natural, harmonic, and melodic variants that differ through alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh scale degree so it can function as a leading tone.
Melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

anchors.quote: The minor key system has three variants: a) Natural, b) Harmonic, and c) Melodic.
The harmonic minor scale includes a raised seventh scale degree
The melodic minor scale includes a raised sixth as well as seventh scale degree.

attribution: Justin Rubin, Music Composition & Theory (2024), chapter 25, University of Minnesota Libraries Publishing

facts: The minor key system has natural, harmonic, and melodic variants that differ through alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh scale degree so it can function as a leading tone.
Melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

keyTerms.df: The minor key system includes variants distinguished through alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
keyTerms.eg: Harmonic minor and melodic minor both involve the seventh scale degree.
keyTerms.mi: The variants differ through alterations to the sixth scale degree rather than the seventh scale degree.
keyTerms.cx: Differences among the variants involve alterations to both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

keyTerms.df: Harmonic minor is a minor-scale variant distinguished by a raised seventh scale degree.
keyTerms.eg: A raised seventh scale degree in harmonic minor can function as a leading tone.
keyTerms.mi: Harmonic minor raises the sixth and seventh scale degrees as its distinguishing alteration.
keyTerms.cx: The paired raising of the sixth and seventh identifies melodic minor; harmonic minor raises the seventh.

keyTerms.df: Melodic minor belongs to the natural, harmonic, and melodic variants of the minor key system.
keyTerms.eg: A passage with raised sixth and seventh scale degrees exemplifies melodic minor.
keyTerms.mi: Melodic minor raises the seventh scale degree in place of raising the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
keyTerms.cx: Melodic minor requires the stated raising of both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

scenario.su: An analyst must classify the provided notations as harmonic minor or melodic minor before a deadline. The labels must be based strictly on the displayed alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
scenario.ma: a passage notation showing a raised seventh scale degree, a comparison notation showing raised sixth and seventh scale degrees

mc.q: A comparison notation shows harmonic minor with a raised seventh scale degree and melodic minor with raised sixth and seventh scale degrees. Which statement defensibly distinguishes these variants?
op: Harmonic raises seventh; melodic raises sixth and seventh
Harmonic raises sixth and seventh; melodic raises seventh
Both raise the sixth and seventh scale degrees
Harmonic raises seventh; melodic raises the sixth
mc.ex: Harmonic minor raises the seventh scale degree, while melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh. Assigning the paired alterations to harmonic minor reverses the supplied distinctions.

mc.q: A notation displays raised sixth and seventh scale degrees, and a deadline requires a label based strictly on those alterations. Which classification is supported by the observation?
op: Classify raised sixth and seventh as melodic minor
Classify raised sixth and seventh as harmonic minor
Classify raised seventh as melodic minor
Classify raised sixth as melodic minor
mc.ex: Raised sixth and seventh scale degrees support classification as melodic minor. Harmonic minor is associated with raising the seventh scale degree so it can function as a leading tone.

facts: The minor key system has natural, harmonic, and melodic variants that differ through alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh scale degree so it can function as a leading tone.
Melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

keyTerms.df: The minor key system encompasses natural, harmonic, and melodic variants that are distinguished by alterations to the sixth and seventh scale degrees.

lessonInput.objectives: Use only the supplied claims to make a defensible distinction without adding outside facts.
lessonInput.topics: Claim 0: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf, with direction constrained by Lenz's law. Claim 1: Induced current direction opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. Claim 2: Changing field strength, area, or orientation can change magnetic flux.

mc.q: A circuit shows changing magnetic flux, an induced emf, and induced current direction opposing the flux change. Which comparison correctly distinguishes Faraday's law from Lenz's law?
op: Faraday links changing flux to emf; Lenz opposes change
Faraday constrains direction; Lenz induces an emf
Faraday opposes change; Lenz links flux to emf
Faraday links changing flux to emf; Lenz supports change
mc.ex: Faraday's law connects changing magnetic flux through a circuit with induced emf, while the induced current direction associated with Lenz's law opposes the producing flux change. Assigning opposition to Faraday and the emf relation to Lenz swaps the supplied relations.

mc.q: A circuit record marks changing field strength while area and orientation are also recorded; the reviewer must select the statement directly supported by these observations. Which classification is warranted?

Changing magnetic flux can change field strength
mc.ex: Changing field strength is listed as able to change magnetic flux. The reversed statement that magnetic flux can change field strength is not supported by the supplied relation.
